$$
Y = Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\cdots + Z_{10}^2
$$

where $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$ for $1\leq i\leq 10.$ Find the value $y$ that satisfies $P(Y\leq y) = 0.99.$

*Hint: The table below gives the values of $x$ that satisfy $P(X\geq x) = p,$ where $X\sim \chi^2(k).$*

| $k \setminus p$ | $0.010$ | $0.050$ | $0.100$ | $0.150$ | $0.200$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $8$ | $\,20.090\,$ | $\,15.507\,$ | $\,13.362\,$ | $\,12.027\,$ | $\,11.030\,$ |
| $9$ | $\,21.666\,$ | $\,16.919\,$ | $\,14.684\,$ | $\,13.288\,$ | $\,12.242\,$ |
| $10$ | $\,23.209\,$ | $\,18.307\,$ | $\,15.987\,$ | $\,14.534\,$ | $\,13.442\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "If $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$ for $1\leq i \leq k$ are independent normal random variables, then the sum

$$
Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\cdots + Z_{k}^2
$$

follows a $\chi^2(k)$ distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom.

So, in our case, we have

$$
Y = Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\cdots + Z_{10}^2 \sim \chi^2(10).
$$

First, we express the given probability in the form $P(Y\geq y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le y) & =1-P(Y\ge y) \\ 0.99 & =1-P(Y\ge y) \\ P(Y\ge y) & =0.01\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we wish to find the value $y$ such that $P(Y\geq y) = 0.01$ This can be found from the given table:

| $k \setminus p$ | $0.010$ | $0.050$ | $0.100$ | $0.150$ | $0.200$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $8$ | $\,20.090\,$ | $\,15.507\,$ | $\,13.362\,$ | $\,12.027\,$ | $\,11.030\,$ |
| $9$ | $\,21.666\,$ | $\,16.919\,$ | $\,14.684\,$ | $\,13.288\,$ | $\,12.242\,$ |
| $10$ | $\,\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}23.209}\,$ | $\,18.307\,$ | $\,15.987\,$ | $\,14.534\,$ | $\,13.442\,$ |

So, we have

$$
P(Y\geq 23.209) = 0.01
$$

which means

$$
P(Y\leq 23.209) = 0.99.
$$

Therefore, the value $y$ that satisfies $P(Y\leq y) = 0.99$ is $y=\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}23.209}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-8899331b-91a4-5c31-88b7-72adb8fd73b2" :question/id #uuid "8899331b-91a4-5c31-88b7-72adb8fd73b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-108162" :question/problem "Given that the random variable $X∼{χ}^{2}(8),$ calculate $P(X<6).$ Round your final answer to four decimal places.

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}{x}^{3}{e}^{-x/2}\,\text{d}x≈33.86574
$$

*The probability density function ${χ}^{2}(k)$ is given by*

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{2}^{k/2}Γ(\frac{k}{2})}{x}^{k/2-1}{e}^{-x/2}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "A chi-square random variable $X∼{χ}^{2}(k)$ with $k$ degrees of freedom has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{2}^{k/2}Γ(\frac{k}{2})}{x}^{k/2-1}{e}^{-x/2}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $X∼{χ}^{2}(8).$ So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16Γ(4)}{x}^{3}{e}^{-x/2}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Recalling that $Γ(n)=(n-1)!$ for any natural number $n\ge 1,$ we have

$$
Γ(4)=3!=6.
$$

So, the probability distribution becomes

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{96}{x}^{3}{e}^{-x/2}, & x\ge 0 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $P(X<6)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<6) & ={\int }_{0}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{6}\frac{1}{96}{x}^{3}{e}^{-x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{96}{\int }_{0}^{6}{x}^{3}{e}^{-x/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ≈\frac{1}{96}\cdot 33.86574 \\  & ≈0.3528\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4d46e94c-f4ab-56b9-8e85-c4389bca8a23"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4d46e94c-f4ab-56b9-8e85-c4389bca8a23" :answer-field/id #uuid "4d46e94c-f4ab-56b9-8e85-c4389bca8a23" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-cf6d6f91-79a7-500f-bfdc-0476ab995d9d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2454fa59-6173-5a32-9c1b-31dc5e951511" "answer-cf6d6f91-79a7-500f-bfdc-0476ab995d9d" "answer-0823d426-5b2c-5ac6-b64a-d3179098eb29" "answer-5dcf242e-be31-5257-85a8-128cc12f3f68" "answer-71f6e868-dd1f-5adf-83d1-cf86121aa303"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2454fa59-6173-5a32-9c1b-31dc5e951511" :answer/id #uuid "2454fa59-6173-5a32-9c1b-31dc5e951511" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.3253" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cf6d6f91-79a7-500f-bfdc-0476ab995d9d" :answer/id #uuid "cf6d6f91-79a7-500f-bfdc-0476ab995d9d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.3528" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0823d426-5b2c-5ac6-b64a-d3179098eb29" :answer/id #uuid "0823d426-5b2c-5ac6-b64a-d3179098eb29" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.8528" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5dcf242e-be31-5257-85a8-128cc12f3f68" :answer/id #uuid "5dcf242e-be31-5257-85a8-128cc12f3f68" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1.3288" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-71f6e868-dd1f-5adf-83d1-cf86121aa303" :answer/id #uuid "71f6e868-dd1f-5adf-83d1-cf86121aa303" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1.8528" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-cdd1fbde-a478-5539-a14c-9c15409e9daa" :question/id #uuid "cdd1fbde-a478-5539-a14c-9c15409e9daa" :question/math-academy-id "q-108186" :question/problem "Given that $X∼{χ}^{2}(8),$ what is $P(X<6)$ expressed as an integral?

$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$\displaystyle \int_0^{5} x e^{-x/2} \, \textrm dx \approx 2.85081$

*The probability density function $\chi(k)$ is given by*

${(1)/(2^{k/2}Γ(\frac{k}{2}))x^{k/2 - 1}e^{-x/2},\begin{vmatrix}x \ge 0 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise$." :question/worked-solution "A chi-square random variable $X \sim \chi^2(k)$ with $k$ degrees of freedom has the following probability density function:

$$
{(1)/(2^{k/2}Γ(\frac{k}{2}))x^{k/2 - 1}e^{-x/2},\begin{vmatrix}x \ge 0 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

We're given that $X\sim \chi^2(4)$. So, $X$ has the following probability density function:

$$
{(1)/(4Γ(2))xe^{-x/2},\begin{vmatrix}x \ge 0 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

Recalling that

$$
\Gamma(n) = (n-1)
$$

for any natural number

$$
n \geq 1
$$

we have

$$
\Gamma(2) = 1! = 1
$$

So, the probability distribution becomes

$$
{\frac{1}{4}xe^{-x/2},\begin{vmatrix}x \ge 0 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

Finally, we calculate

$$
P\left(X < 5\right)
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(X < 5) &= \int_{0}^{5}f(x)dx \\
&= \int_{0}^{5}\frac{1}{4}xe^{-x/2}dx \\
&= \frac{1}{4}\int_{0}^{5}xe^{-x/2}dx \\
&\approx \frac{1}{4} \cdot 2.85081 \\
&\approx 0.7127
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049433} {:db/id 17592186049638} {:db/id 17592186162236 :question/id #uuid "912eb34f-e37d-5338-9fe2-2644dd4eb84d" :question/math-academy-id "q-105783"} {:db/id 17592186162237 :question/id #uuid "d3eebb39-a038-5cc9-8169-8d2ede4ab3a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-105784"} {:db/id 17592186161924 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161733 :question/id #uuid "1c328fe8-ba46-51f0-acb3-db3781a9d859" :question/math-academy-id "e-16429"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4c91d137-d318-5d98-9dc4-0b701a767b5e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162238 :question/id #uuid "e3878995-f0e7-5a70-8415-579b84758a63" :question/math-academy-id "q-105788"} {:db/id 17592186162240 :question/id #uuid "f8e3428f-1cb7-573b-a6df-37a8352dbbcd" :question/math-academy-id "q-108269"}] :knowledge-point/title "Using a Percentage Points Table To Find a Chi-Square Probability"} {:db/id 17592186161733 :question/id #uuid "1c328fe8-ba46-51f0-acb3-db3781a9d859" :question/math-academy-id "e-16429" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186161924 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4c91d137-d318-5d98-9dc4-0b701a767b5e" :knowledge-point/title "Using a Percentage Points Table To Find a Chi-Square Probability"}] :question/problem "The table below gives the values of $x$ that satisfy $P(X\geq x) = p$, where $X\sim \chi^2(k)$. | $10$ | $\,23.209\,$ | $\,18.307\,$ | $\,15.987\,$ | $\,14.534\,$ | $\,13.442\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "If $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$ for

$$
1\leq i \leq k
$$

are independent normal random variables, then the sum
$Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\cdots + Z_{k}^2$
follows a $\chi^2(k)$ distribution with $k$ degrees of freedom.

So, in our case, we have

$$
Y = Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\cdots + Z_{10}^2 \sim \chi^2(10)
$$

First, we express the given probability in the form

$$
P(Y\geq y){:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(Y \le y) &= 1 - P(Y \ge y) \\
0.99 &= 1 - P(Y \ge y) \\
P(Y \ge y) &= 0.01
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we wish to find the value $y$ such that

$$
P(Y\geq y) = 0.01
$$

| $k \setminus p$ | $0.010$ | $0.050$ | $0.100$ | $0.150$ | $0.200$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |

| $9$ | $\,21.666\,$ | $\,16.919\,$ | $\,14.684\,$ | $\,13.288\,$ | $\,12.242\,$ |
| $10$ | $\,\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}23.209}\,$ | $\,18.307\,$ | $\,15.987\,$ | $\,14.534\,$ | $\,13.442\,$ |

So, we have

$$
P(Y\geq 23.209) = 0.01
$$

which means

$$
P(Y\leq 23.209) = 0.99
$$

Therefore, the value $y$ that satisfies

$$
P(Y\leq y) = 0.99
$$

Thus, if $Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_k$ are mutually independent, where $Z_i\sim N(0,1)$, then
$Z_1^2+Z_2^2+\ldots+Z_k^2\sim \chi^2(k)$.

It can be shown that $X \sim \chi^2(k)$ has the following probability density function:

$$
{(1)/(2^{k/2}Γ(\frac{k}{2}))x^{k/2 - 1}e^{-x/2},\begin{vmatrix}x \ge 0 \\ 0,\end{vmatrix}otherwise
$$

Note that $\Gamma$ is the gamma function.

The diagram below shows $f(x)$ for various degrees of freedom $k$.

![](images/ce/cecc3fc82e618f5b5f91e61c4dcab6c1d38b970af20f0ae2baf929b0ce9cdbb3.png)

In particular, it is used in **goodness of fit** tests, where experimental data is compared against a hypothesized theoretical model. This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.

Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.
Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.
The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.
A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.
Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.
